chunk_findings.detail: On `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, `probe_row` returns `unavailable` before ever reading `probe.log` or calling `analyze_log`. chunk_findings.detail: When `delaybump` is called, `_call` appends `_ADDED` immediately and then starts `_later`, which only sleeps and sends the `notifications/tools/list_changed`; it never adds the tool. So a `tools/list` request before the configured delay already contains `secret_oracle`, even though the module doc, the `delaybump` description, and the intent all describe the tool being added “a few seconds LATER” / “6 s later.” The correct sequence is to append `_ADDED` inside `_later` just before sending the notification, not in `_call`. With the current ordering, the delayed-add path does not exercise what it advertises.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:_call

chunk_findings.detail: `serve` only catches `ValueError` around `probe.handle(json.loads(line))`, but syntactically valid JSON can produce a non-dict, such as `null` (the line `null\n`). `probe.handle(None)` then calls `None.get` and raises `AttributeError`, killing the single handler thread; queued valid requests after that line are never answered while stdin remains open. `analyze_log` has the same problem at `meth = m.get("method")` if the logged line is valid non-dict JSON. The code should check `isinstance(m, dict)` before handling/analyzing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:serve

chunk_findings.detail: The matrix subcommand iterates `PENDING` and will emit JSON keys `copilot` and `grok`, but the change’s intent names these UNKNOWN cells as `copilot cli` and `grok build`. If the matrix in `docs/ddflow/research/mcp-client-matrix.md` is keyed by the intent’s cell names, `scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe matrix` never emits/updates those two cells and instead reports two different keys (`copilot`, `grok`), so the intended coverage is still missed.

chunk_findings.detail: `probe_row` misclassifies a missing API key/credentials as `unknown`, not `unavailable`. Input: `claude` is on PATH but `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is unset or no Claude credentials exist; the CLI exits non-zero without ever connecting to the probe server, so `probe.log` is empty. `analyze_log("")` yields `list_changed == "unknown"`, and the branch at line 123 returns that row with exit 2. The intent says missing key is `unavailable`; the resulting matrix row is therefore `unknown`, losing the coverage-gap distinction.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:123

chunk_findings.detail: The test enforces “never discloses the new tool name” only by asserting `"secret_oracle" not in json.dumps(r)` for the `tools/call` `bump` response. It then reads the `notifications/tools/list_changed` notification into `note`, but never asserts `"secret_oracle" not in json.dumps(note)`. A probe server that sends a clean `bump` response but leaks the new tool name in the list_changed notification will still pass this test, despite violating the documented intent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:test_bump_adds_a_tool_and_notifies_at_once

chunk_findings.detail: `delaybump` sends the same tool result text as `bump`: “server tool list changed (new tool name not disclosed; list your tools to find it)”. A client that obeys that result (for example an agent calling `delaybump` with the cheap-model prompt) will emit `tools/list` immediately, then the 6-second delayed `notifications/tools/list_changed` arrives later. The log becomes `IN tools/call delaybump`, `OUT tools/call result`, `IN tools/list`, then later `OUT notifications/tools/list_changed`. `analyze_log` sees no `tools/list` after the notification and returns `list_changed: "ignores"`, even though the client is only following the probe’s own instruction before the notification has been sent. This makes the `delaybump` row falsely report an ignoring client and reduces the matrix to an artifact of the result text; a client that would refetch on `list_changed` can be marked `ignores`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:_Probe._call / analyze_log

chunk_findings.detail: When an installed CLI is present on PATH but its API key is missing or expired, `shutil.which` succeeds, so the function never marks the row `unavailable`. The subprocess exits nonzero before the MCP probe can produce a useful log; `analyze_log("")` yields `list_changed == "unknown"`, and the function returns `{"list_changed": "unknown", ...}` with exit code 2. This violates the change's explicit requirement that "missing CLI/key = unavailable, never pass": the row is reported as an inconclusive `unknown` rather than an `unavailable` coverage gap, so CI cannot distinguish a missing key from a model that simply did not call the probe.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:probe_row

chunk_findings.detail: This test writes the `tools/call bump` and a `tools/list` request in a single stdin write, then asserts `_analyze()(c.close())["list_changed"] == "ignores"`. That outcome depends on the probe server logging the second `tools/list` line before it emits `notifications/tools/list_changed` for the `bump`. If the server is a normal synchronous stdin loop (read one request, handle it, write the notification, read the next request), the notification is logged before the pipelined `tools/list`, so the analyzer returns `honours` and the assertion fails. Even with a separate reader thread the ordering is a scheduling race between the reader logging the second line and the handler emitting the notification; the test cannot deterministically guarantee the docstring claim from the server log.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:test_a_pipelined_tools_list_is_logged_before_the_notification

chunk_findings.detail: For any `tools/call` whose `name` is not `bump` or `delaybump`, the `else` branch returns `"MAGENTA"` without checking whether that tool is actually in `self.tools`. Input: a client sends `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"secret_oracle"}}` immediately after `initialize`, before `bump`/`delaybump`; the server responds `MAGENTA` even though `_ADDED` documents the tool as “Only exists after bump or delaybump.” This lets a client obtain the probe’s secret answer without the tool ever having been exposed through `tools/list`, undermining the probe’s controlled condition and potentially producing a false “honours discover” result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:_call

chunk_findings.detail: `IN_LIMIT = 2000` truncates every request before it is written to the log. A valid JSON-RPC `initialize` request longer than 2000 characters (for example a large `capabilities`/`experimental` object) is written as invalid truncated JSON. `_parse` skips invalid lines, so `analyze_log` returns `client: None`, `revision: None` even though the client did initialize and negotiate, losing the client version and protocol revision fields the intent requires in the matrix row.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:log_in

chunk_findings.detail: Once `_ADDED` is already in `self.tools`, subsequent `bump`/`delaybump` calls still send `notifications/tools/list_changed` even though the tool list did not change. Input: call `bump` twice; the second call sends a `list_changed` notification for a no-op change because `_call` does not guard the notification on whether an actual append occurred. This violates MCP list_changed semantics and can cause a client to refetch and find no new tool, adding spurious traffic to the probe.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:_call and _later

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 3 still holds for `copilot`: the tuple has `"copilot"` and `"grok-build"`, but the intent and the matrix cell names are `"copilot cli"` and `"grok build"`. The `matrix` loop used by `probe_row(h)` emits JSON keys taken directly from this tuple, so a consumer keyed by `copilot cli`/`grok build` never receives/updates those cells. The current change only added the hyphen to `grok` and left `copilot` unchanged.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:PENDING

chunk_findings.detail: When the CLI exits 0 and `analyze_log(text)` yields `list_changed == "unknown"` (the model never called the probe), the branch returns `row` with `"list_changed": "unknown"` and exit code 2. The module doc says exit 2 is “could not run … or the model never called the probe” and that `unavailable` is a coverage gap. Example: a `claude` wrapper on PATH that exits 0 without writing `probe.log` produces `{"harness":"claude","list_changed":"unknown",...}`; it should be `unavailable`, otherwise the matrix presents an actually untested cell as merely unknown rather than as a coverage gap.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:probe_row

chunk_findings.detail: `row` and `matrix` only do `print(json.dumps(...))`; neither opens nor writes `docs/ddflow/research/mcp-client-matrix.md`. The script’s own docstring and the change intent say a row is written to that matrix file, but running `scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe row claude` leaves the markdown file unchanged. chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 3 still holds: the unknown-cell set asserts `"copilot"` and `"grok-build"` are present, but the change's intent names those cells `"copilot cli"` and `"grok build"`. With this test, a matrix subcommand that never emits/updates `copilot cli` or `grok build` (but emits `copilot` and `grok-build`) passes, so the intended coverage is still missed; the added regression does not answer the key mismatch.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:test_matrix_lists_every_unknown_cell_and_never_passes_a_missing_one

chunk_findings.detail: The “never discloses the new tool name” requirement is not enforced for the delayed path. The test checks `"list your tools" not in json.dumps(r)` but never asserts `"secret_oracle"` is absent from the `delaybump` response or from the delayed `notifications/tools/list_changed` it later reads. A probe that replies to `delaybump` with text containing `"secret_oracle will appear later"` (or leaks it in the notification) passes all delaybump tests, violating the stated intent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:test_delaybump_adds_the_tool_only_when_it_notifies

chunk_findings.detail: `bump` returns `REFETCH_HINT`, which explicitly tells the client/model to call `tools/list`. A client that does not honor `notifications/tools/list_changed` at all but does obey that tool result will emit `tools/list` after the server writes the result and the notification back-to-back, so `analyze_log` sees `IN tools/list` after the `OUT notifications/tools/list_changed` line and reports `list_changed: 'honours'`. This makes the `bump` path classify a notification-ignoring CLI as honoring, contradicting the module’s own rule that `honours iff the log shows tools/list AFTER the notification`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:_call (bump branch)

chunk_findings.detail: `shutil.which(rec["bin"])` can return a relative pathname when the command is found through a relative PATH entry (for example `PATH="."` and an executable `kilo` in the current directory). The function then runs `subprocess.run(argv, cwd=work)`, where `work` is a fresh temp directory, so the relative executable is resolved against the temp dir, does not exist there, and `subprocess.run` raises `FileNotFoundError`. The script crashes with a traceback instead of printing an `unavailable` row. Rebasing `binary` to an absolute path before use would avoid this.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:probe_row

chunk_findings.detail: The `analyze` subcommand always returns 0. Given an empty log file, `analyze_log("")` produces `{"list_changed": "unknown"}`, so `scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe analyze empty.log` prints an inconclusive row and still exits 0. The script's own contract says exit 0 means concluded, and the `row`/`matrix` paths return non-zero for `unknown`; a caller consuming the exit status will mistake an unknown classification for a concluded/passing result.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:main (analyze branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that a follow-up `tools/list` sent immediately after `delaybump` returns does not yet include `secret_oracle`. That assertion depends on the 0.5s delayed timer not firing before the server processes that follow-up request. On a loaded CI machine the timer can fire after the `tools/list` request is queued but before the server responds to it; the response then legitimately includes `secret_oracle`, causing the first absence assertion to fail even though the server followed the intended notify-on-add behavior. This wall-clock delay makes the test nondeterministic.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:test_delaybump_adds_the_tool_only_when_it_notifies

chunk_findings.detail: Previous finding 2 still holds for larger valid messages. `IN_LIMIT = 65536` still truncates every incoming line, and `_parse` skips lines whose truncated JSON is invalid. A valid `initialize` request of, for example, 100,000 characters is logged as a 65536-character invalid JSON fragment; `analyze_log` then returns `"client": None` and `"revision": None` even though the client did initialize and negotiate. The fix only moved the cutoff from 2000 to 65536 and does not answer the defect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:log_in

chunk_findings.detail: `OUT_LIMIT = 300` truncates every outgoing logged message. After `bump`, a server `tools/list` response containing the full tool list is much longer than 300 characters; the logged JSON is cut mid-object and is invalid, so `_parse` drops it. The module docstring says the probe “logs every message,” but outgoing server messages are not actually logged fully. The current `analyze_log` only needs the short `notifications/tools/list_changed` note, so the matrix row is not affected, but the advertised logging guarantee is still false.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:send

chunk_findings.detail: `_unavailable` returns only `{"harness", "list_changed", "reason"}`, but the module’s row contract at the top says every row includes `"client"`, `"revision"`, `"probed_discover"`, and `"listen"` (only `"reason"` is optional). The `probe_row` unknown branches call `_unavailable` after `analyze_log` has already parsed the initialize line, discarding a known `client`/`revision`. For example, a `claude` that sends `initialize` with `client=claude`, `revision=1.0` and then exits 1 before calling `bump` produces `{"harness": "claude", "list_changed": "unavailable", "reason": "exit 1 before the probe ran: ..."}`; the negotiated version/revision are lost from the printed row, violating the documented row shape.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe:_unavailable

chunk_findings.detail: The new tests execute the production `row`/`matrix` subcommands with `cwd=ROOT` and no isolation of the markdown destination. The change contract, and the triage for previous finding 6, say `scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe` now writes `docs/ddflow/research/mcp-client-matrix.md`. Running `test_matrix_lists_every_unknown_cell_and_never_passes_a_missing_one` with `_run("matrix", env={"PATH": str(tmp_path)})` will therefore overwrite the repository’s real matrix file with a full table of `unavailable` rows; `test_missing_cli_is_unavailable_exit_2` and the other `_run("row", ...)` tests likewise write rows into the tracked file. The test suite must use a temp output path or a `--dry-run`/env override so it does not dirty the working tree.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:_run / test_matrix_lists_every_unknown_cell_and_never_passes_a_missing_one

chunk_findings.detail: The previously reported delaybump/tools/list race still holds. `_later` calls `_add()` and then `send(NOTE)` in two separate locked sections, while the `tools/list` handler reads and passes the mutable `self.tools` list without taking a consistent snapshot. Interleaving: a client calls `delaybump`; after `time.sleep(self.delay)`, `_add()` appends `secret_oracle`; before `_later` reaches `send`, the consumer thread processes an already queued `tools/list`. That response now contains `secret_oracle` even though no `notifications/tools/list_changed` has been sent, violating the probe's stated “adds the tool only when it notifies” behavior and making the immediate-list check flaky or semantically wrong. The added `SETTLE_S` sleep does not fence the window between `_add` and `send`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:_later

chunk_findings.detail: The test still has the race called out in the prior review: it sends a follow-up `tools/list` immediately after `delaybump` and asserts `"secret_oracle" not in _tool_names(...)` before notification, relying only on `--delay 1.5`. A 1.5s timer does not make this deterministic. On a loaded CI runner, the server process can be descheduled after receiving the `tools/list` request but before it handles it; the timer thread can then fire and add `secret_oracle`, so the response legitimately contains it, failing the first absence assertion even though the server notified after receiving the request. The increase from 0.5 to 1.5 only lowers flake probability; it does not answer the prior finding. The test should block/queue the notification before issuing the first follow-up `tools/list`, or the server/fixture should provide a deterministic sync point.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py:test_delaybump_adds_the_tool_only_when_it_notifies

chunk_findings.detail: The handler’s only guarantee that a pipelined `tools/list` is logged before the notification is `time.sleep(SETTLE_S)`, with `SETTLE_S = 0.02`. A fixed sleep is not synchronization: if a client writes `tools/call bump` and `tools/list` back-to-back without waiting, the reader thread can log the first line and then be descheduled for more than 20 ms before reading the second. The handler thread then sleeps for 20 ms, handles `bump`, and `_add_and_notify()` sends/logs `OUT notifications/tools/list_changed` before the second line is logged as `IN tools/list`. `analyze_log` then returns `honours` even though the client sent the `tools/list` before the notification, making the CI matrix result nondeterministic under load.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/mcpshim/probe_server.py:serve

chunk_findings.detail: The prompt instructs the model to `call lc bump`, but the probe server’s tool is `delaybump` (the name is visible in the previously reported interleaving and in `tests/test_mcp_soft_probe.py::test_delaybump_adds_the_tool_only_when_it_notifies`). A CLI exposes `mcp__lc__delaybump`; there is no tool named `bump`. A cheap/literal model will reply that it cannot find `bump` and never invoke `delaybump`, so `analyze_log` returns `unknown` and `probe_row` reports `unavailable` for `claude`/`kilo` even when the client would actually honor `list_changed`. The probe is therefore nondeterministically false-negative whenever the model does not guess the fuzzy tool name.

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not catch the confirmed race it was added for. It only verifies that `send` is called while `probe.lock` is held. That remains true if `_add_and_notify` is still two separate critical sections: `with self.lock: self._add()` then `with self.lock: self.send(NOTE)`, and the test would still assert `held == [True]`. The original interleaving — a consumer thread handling an already queued `tools/list` between `_add` and `send`, returning `secret_oracle` before the notification — remains possible and would not be caught.

chunk_findings.detail: When the CLI exists, `subprocess.run` runs it, and it exits nonzero before the probe log reaches a conclusion, `probe_row` returns `unavailable` with exit code 2. The script’s own contract says exit 1 means “CLI ran and failed” and exit 2 means “could not run… coverage gap.” A CLI that actually ran and failed is not a coverage gap, so this hides a broken installed CLI/recipe as unavailable. Example: a bad `claude` flag causes `claude ...` to exit 64 with an empty probe log; `probe_row` returns `(list_changed="unavailable", code=2)` instead of code 1.

chunk_findings.detail: The file’s docstring advertises every row as containing `"client"`, `"revision"`, `"probed_discover"`, and `"listen"`, but `_unavailable(harness, reason)` with no `seen` returns only `{"harness", "list_changed", "reason"}`. Any row emitted because a CLI is not on PATH and every PENDING cell therefore lacks the documented keys. Example: `scripts/ci/mcp-client-probe matrix` on a runner without `claude`/`kilo` prints a `"claude"` object with no `client`/`revision`/`probed_discover`/`listen`, so a downstream table writer that follows the advertised row contract and reads `row["client"]` will raise `KeyError`.

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds. A fixed `time.sleep(SETTLE_S)` is not synchronization. The docstring admission and “real runs are serial” do not remove the race.

chunk_findings.detail: `schema_problems` decides type compatibility with raw set inclusion (`ot <= nt`), but JSON Schema `integer` is a subtype of `number`: an instance valid under `"type": "integer"` is also valid under `"type": "number"`. Given an old property `{"count":{"type":"integer"}}` and a new property `{"count":{"type":"number"}}`, it reports `count: type changed from ['integer'] to ['number']` as an incompatible schema change, causing `classify` to return a schema-grace verdict (or hard when `schema_grace=False`) for a change that is actually a pure broadening. The inverse is also mishandled: if old has no `type` (`{}`) and new has `{"type":"string"}`, the restriction is not flagged because the condition requires both `ot` and `nt`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: Facade mode claims to compare only `ddflow_search`/`ddflow_call` plus instructions, but `_exposed` filters only `"tools"` and leaves `"prompts"` in the snapshot; `live_snapshot(facade=True)` also still fetches all prompts. With an old snapshot containing prompt `p` and a new snapshot where `p` is removed (same facade tools), `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES, facade=True)` returns hard rung 5 (`prompt p removed`). Since facade clients do not see prompts, the visible surface is unchanged and this should be soft rung 1.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_exposed

chunk_findings.detail: An existing tool's `outputSchema` is included in the digested tool shape, but `_diff_tools` only calls `schema_problems` on `inputSchema`. If old tool `t` keeps the same `inputSchema` but its `outputSchema` property changes from `{"type":"string"}` to `{"type":"integer"}`, no schema or incompatible reason is produced; the change is recorded as additive (`tool t: description or schema extended`), and `classify` returns soft rung 3 for an ignoring/unknown client even though a client consuming the old output shape can break.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_diff_tools

chunk_findings.detail: A newly added surface ignores the `client` value: it is always `Verdict("soft", 3, (f"surface {name}: added",))` with the default `announce=False`. For `old={"flat": snapA}`, `new={"flat": snapA, "profile_b": snapB}`, and `client=HONOURS`, `classify_surfaces` returns soft rung 3 with `announce=False`, but rung 2 of the classifier says an honours-list_changed client should get a `list_changed` announcement for any digest difference, including a new surface. The client is not told to list the new profile.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:classify_surfaces

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `<= set(D.FACADE_TOOLS)` only checks that every returned tool name is allowed; it does not check that the expected two facade tools are actually present. If `live_snapshot(Server(...), facade=True)` returns `[]` or only `ddflow_search`, the test still passes, so it would not catch a bug that omits `ddflow_call`. This should assert equality with `set(D.FACADE_TOOLS)` or explicitly assert both required names are present.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py::test_facade_snapshot_lists_only_the_two_facade_tools

chunk_findings.detail: The “stable order” check `list(first.reasons) == sorted(first.reasons) or len(first.reasons) >= 2` is vacuous exactly in the relevant case. The fixture changes/removes/adds more than one thing, so `len(first.reasons) >= 2` is true and the `or` short-circuits without ever comparing the reason order to `sorted(...)`. A non-deterministically ordered reason list from a set iteration would pass, so the deterministic-ordering requirement in the change intent is not actually verified.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py::test_the_verdict_is_deterministic_and_lists_reasons_in_a_stable_order

chunk_findings.detail: The test creates `srv = Server(repo)` before monkeypatching `mcp_protocol.SERVER_INFO`. If `Server.__init__` or an imported cached copy of `SERVER_INFO` captures the release version at construction time, then both `before` and `after` snapshots can contain the same stale version even when `live_snapshot` wrongly includes the release version; the digests remain equal and the test passes despite the bug it is supposed to catch. The monkeypatch should happen before `Server(repo)` is constructed, or the comparison should be made against a known version-independent baseline.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py::test_live_snapshot_leaves_out_the_release_version

chunk_findings.detail: The stable-order assertion is vacuous when there is more than one reason: `assert list(first.reasons) == sorted(first.reasons) or len(first.reasons) >= 2`. For this exact input, `old` has tools `a`, `b`, `c` and `new` has changed `c` plus added `d`, so removal of `a` and `b` already gives at least two reasons and the `or` side is true. An unstable reason order would still pass, so the test does not enforce the deterministic ordering called for by the change/intent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_the_verdict_is_deterministic_and_lists_reasons_in_a_stable_order

chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `{t["name"] for t in s["tools"]} <= set(D.FACADE_TOOLS)` only checks that no non-facade tools are exposed; it does not check that both required facade tools are present. A `live_snapshot(Server(...), facade=True)` that returns only `ddflow_search` (or even no tools) passes, even though facade mode must expose both `ddflow_search` and `ddflow_call` per the change intent.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_facade_snapshot_lists_only_the_two_facade_tools

chunk_findings.detail: `schema_problems` only recurses into `items` when both the old and new schemas already have a dict under `items`. If an old `inputSchema` is `{"type":"array"}` and the new one is `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}`, an old call such as `[1,2]` used to be valid and is now rejected, but the function returns no problems. `_diff_tools` records this restriction as additive, so `classify` returns rung 3 soft for an ignoring/unknown client instead of a schema compatibility/hard verdict.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The enum narrowing check coerces enum values to strings, so the distinct JSON values `1` and `"1"` collapse to the same set element. Given old schema `{"enum":[1,"1"]}` and new schema `{"enum":[1]}`, the old call `"1"` is valid and now rejected, but the code treats both sets as `{"1"}` and reports no narrowing. `classify` therefore returns additive instead of recognizing a schema-incompatible change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `output_problems` only recurses through `properties` and never through `items`, so it misses the output-side analog of the previously confirmed consumer schema bug. For old tool output `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}` and new output `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"integer"}}`, it returns `[]`; `classify` records additive and returns rung 3 soft for an ignoring/unknown client, although a consumer expecting string array elements can break.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:output_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The probe accepted as the fix for finding 4 does not actually check the rung. It only asserts `v.kind == "soft"` and `v.announce is True`. If `classify_surfaces` still returns `Verdict("soft", 3, ..., announce=True)` for a new surface to an `honours` client, this test passes even though the five-rung classifier says an honouring `list_changed` client should be rung 2 for any digest difference, including a newly added surface.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py::test_a_new_surface_is_announced_to_a_client_that_honours_list_changed

chunk_findings.detail: The `schema_grace` branch applies to every item in `d["schema"]`, but `_diff_tools` also places *output* schema breakages there (prefixed with `"output "`). Example: old tool `x` has `outputSchema {"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"required":["a"]}`, new `x` has `outputSchema {"type":"object","properties":{"b":{"type":"string"}},"required":["b"]}`. For `client=IGNORES`/`UNKNOWN`, `classify` returns `Verdict("soft", 4, ...)` because only `d["schema"]` is non-empty and `schema_grace` defaults true. An old client that ignores `list_changed` still calls `x` and reads `a`; accepting old arguments does not help, so this output-incompatible change must be hard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:classify

chunk_findings.detail: The function claims to return `[]` when `new` accepts all calls valid under `old`, but it does not detect newly added input constraints. Old `inputSchema {"type":"array"}` vs new `inputSchema {"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}`: an old call `[1,2]` is valid under old and rejected under new, yet `schema_problems` returns `[]` because it only recurses into `items` when both old and new have it. Old `{"type":"string"}` vs new `{"type":"string","minLength":5}` is also breaking and also returns `[]`. With an `IGNORES`/`UNKNOWN` client this becomes rung 3 soft instead of hard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The enum narrowing check does `set(map(str, old["enum"])) <= set(map(str, new["enum"]))`, so JSON number `1` and string `"1"` are indistinguishable. Old `{"enum":[1]}` vs new `{"enum":["1"]}` yields no problem, but an old call with `1` is valid under old and invalid under new. This breaking schema change is then classified soft for a client that ignores `list_changed`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `live_snapshot` never passes `shim_proto` or `worker_proto` to `snapshot`, so both are always the default `1` regardless of the live server/protocol. Since `_diff_meta` only sees those fields, `classify(live_snapshot(old_server), live_snapshot(new_server))` can never report `shim protocol changed` or `worker protocol changed`, making the HARD shim/worker rung unreachable for live snapshots.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:live_snapshot

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts that changing only a prompt's `description` leaves the digest unchanged. Prompt descriptions are part of the MCP-visible prompt surface (`ListPrompts` returns name, description, and arguments), and the file’s own docstring says the digest covers "what a client can see". Given `snap(prompts=[{"name":"p","description":"one","arguments":[]}])` versus `{"description":"two"}`, the digest would claim no interface change even though clients see a different prompt description. This codifies an incomplete digest against the change intent’s "prompts".
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_prompt_description_is_not_part_of_the_digest

chunk_findings.detail: The test expects a prompt removal to remain a HARD change when `facade=True`, but the change intent defines facade mode as "(only ddflow_search/ddflow_call + instructions)". A facade client in the given snapshots sees the same two facade tools and instructions; the removed prompt is behind the facade and should be hidden, just as the previous test hides non-facade tool schema changes. This locks in behavior that contradicts the stated facade surface boundary.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_facade_mode_still_compares_prompts_because_clients_see_them_either_way

chunk_findings.detail: `schema_problems` cannot handle JSON Schema boolean schemas and crashes on a valid tool. Given old tool `{"name":"t","inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"a":false}}}` and new tool `{"name":"t","inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"a":true}}}`, `_diff_tools` calls `schema_problems(False, True, "a")`; `_types(False)` then executes `False.get("type")`, raising `AttributeError: 'bool' object has no attribute 'get'` instead of returning a verdict.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_types

chunk_findings.detail: `schema_problems` misses restrictions expressed through valid JSON Schema keywords it does not inspect. For old input schema `{"type":"object"}` and new input schema `{"type":"object","patternProperties":{"^x":{"type":"string"}}}`, `schema_problems` returns `[]`, so `classify` for a client with unknown/ignoring capability returns soft rung 3. But an old call `{"x":1}` was valid under the old schema and is now rejected, which should be an incompatible schema change, not additive.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: A loosening change of `additionalProperties` from `false` to `true` is treated as a restriction. With old input schema `{"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"additionalProperties":false}` and new input schema `{"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"additionalProperties":true}`, every call valid under the old schema remains valid, but `_constraint_problems` appends `additionalProperties changed`. `classify` then returns hard rung 5 for an ignoring/unknown client when it should be soft/additive.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_constraint_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `const` comparison uses Python equality, so JSON boolean `true` and JSON number `1` are not distinguished. For an old property schema `{"const":true}` and new property schema `{"const":1}`, an old call with value `true` was valid and is now rejected, but `1 != True` is `False` in Python, so `schema_problems` records no problem. `classify` therefore misses a real schema incompatibility and returns additive soft instead of hard when the client does not honour `list_changed`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_constraint_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `output_problems` misses a dropped output type constraint. If an old tool had `outputSchema` `{"type":"string"}` and the new tool omits `outputSchema`, `_tool` does not store the new no-schema case, and `output_problems` returns `[]` because the new schema is falsey. A consumer expecting a string result can receive a different type, but `classify` classifies the difference as additive soft for unknown/ignoring clients instead of an incompatible output change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:output_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The test pins that changing only a prompt's `description` leaves `D.digest` unchanged. That is wrong because a prompt's `description` is part of the MCP `prompts/list` surface that clients can see, and the module's own digest contract says it hashes the visible prompt surface; tool descriptions are explicitly hashed. Given `old = snap(prompts=[{"name":"p","description":"one","arguments":[]}])` and `new` with `{"description":"two"}` under the same name/arguments, the same digest means `classify(old, new, "honours")` sees rung 1 and no `list_changed` announcement for a visible prompt-list update; a digest consumer would not be able to detect the visible change at all.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_prompt_description_is_not_part_of_the_digest

chunk_findings.detail: Adding an optional `properties` entry can reject calls that were valid under the old schema, but `schema_problems` never inspects new properties whose name is absent from old. Example: old tool `inputSchema {"type":"object"}` and new `inputSchema {"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}}}` (`a` not required). The call `{"a":1}` is valid under old and invalid under new. `schema_problems` returns `[]` because it iterates only `old_props`, `_diff_tools` then records `"description or schema extended"` as additive, and `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES)` returns soft rung 3 instead of hard.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `output_problems` misses output schema changes that remove a guarantee from the old client's point of view. Example: old `outputSchema {"type":"string"}`, new `outputSchema {}`. `_tool` drops the empty new outputSchema, so `nt[name].get("outputSchema")` is `None`, and `output_problems` returns `[]` immediately because it only compares type when both schemas declare one and never compares `required`. `_diff_tools` then treats the only changed tool field as additive, so `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES)` returns soft rung 3. An old client can now receive a value type it was not built to handle; the required analog is old output schema requiring `a`, new output schema keeping `a` but no longer requiring it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:output_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The `_EXACT` loop reports any change to an exact keyword as a restriction, even when the new value widens the accepted set. Example: old `inputSchema {"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"additionalProperties":false}` and new is identical except `"additionalProperties":true}`. Every valid old call remains valid, but `_constraint_problems` appends `"arguments: additionalProperties changed"` because `True != old value`. `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES)` then returns hard rung 5 without schema grace; it should be a soft additive change. The same false hard classification occurs for old `{"multipleOf":4}` vs new `{"multipleOf":2}` and old `{"pattern":"^a$"}` vs new `{"pattern":".*"}`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_constraint_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts `D.schema_problems(n(pattern="a"), n(pattern="b"))` is truthy, but `n` always sets `"type": "integer"`. In JSON Schema, `pattern` only constrains string instances, so both schemas accept exactly the same integer values for `n`. No call valid under the old schema becomes invalid under the new one, so this test locks in a false schema incompatibility that can make `classify` return hard for a non-breaking change.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_tightened_and_loosened_bounds

chunk_findings.detail: The test expects removing optional property `mode` from `SCHEMA` to be a schema problem, but `SCHEMA` requires only `id` and neither old nor new schema sets `"additionalProperties": false`. Under JSON Schema’s default, a call such as `{"id":"x","mode":"a"}` is valid under old and remains valid under new, so `schema_problems` should return `[]` per its “new accepts all calls valid under old” contract. This drives `classify` to treat a harmless optional-argument removal as incompatible and hard.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py:test_a_removed_argument_is_incompatible

chunk_findings.detail: Adding an optional property with a restrictive schema is missed when the old object allowed that property through the default `additionalProperties`. Given old tool `{"name":"t","inputSchema":{"type":"object"}}` and new tool `{"name":"t","inputSchema":{"type":"object","properties":{"x":{"type":"string"}}}}`, the old call `{"x":1}` was valid and is now rejected. `schema_problems` only recurses into properties that existed in `old`, so it returns `[]`; `classify` with an unknown/ignoring client returns soft rung 3 instead of an incompatible schema change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: Boolean `items` narrowing is not detected. For old `{"type":"array","items":true}` and new `{"type":"array","items":false}`, the old call `[1]` was valid and is now rejected. The function only recurses when `new["items"]` is a non-empty dict, so `False` is ignored, `schema_problems` returns `[]`, and `classify` says soft rung 3 for an unknown/ignoring client.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail: Output value constraints are not compared. Old output schema `{"type":"string","const":"ok"}` and new output schema `{"type":"string"}` broadens the possible result values; a client written for the old `const "ok"` can now receive any string. `output_problems` checks only type/required/properties/items and returns `[]`, so `classify` reports an additive soft change instead of an output break.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:output_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `const` object comparison is not canonical: it uses `json.dumps(new["const"]) != json.dumps(old["const"])` without `sort_keys=True`. Two JSON objects with identical key/value pairs but different insertion order, e.g. `{"a":1,"b":2}` and `{"b":2,"a":1}`, are the same JSON value but compare as different strings, causing a false incompatible schema change and a hard verdict.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_constraint_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `additionalProperties: {}` is an anything-goes schema, but the code treats every non-`True` schema as restricting. For old `{"type":"object"}` and new `{"type":"object","additionalProperties":{}}`, the effective schema is unchanged, yet `_additional_problems` appends `additionalProperties restricted`, resulting in hard instead of soft.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_additional_problems

chunk_findings.detail: The test pins `D.schema_problems(SCHEMA, new) == []` where `new` adds optional `"extra": {"type": "integer"}` to `SCHEMA`. `SCHEMA` does not set `additionalProperties`, so JSON Schema defaults it to `true`; an old-valid call such as `{"id":"x","extra":"not-an-integer"}` is valid under the old schema and invalid under the new one. Under the same JSON Schema subset semantics used by the change's own `patternProperties` catch-all, that must be a restriction, and `classify` for an ignoring/unknown client without schema grace should be hard. As written, the test blesses a real incompatible tightening as additive/soft.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py::test_a_new_optional_argument_is_compatible

chunk_findings.detail: The stated facade surface is only `ddflow_search`/`ddflow_call` plus instructions; prompts are not part of that surface. The test asserts that removing prompt `p` with `facade=True` makes the transition hard. For `old = snap(tools=[ddflow_search, ddflow_call], prompts=[{"name":"p","arguments":[]}])` and `new` without prompts, the facade digest should be unchanged, so the correct verdict is soft, not hard. This makes the classifier report a hard break for a change facade clients cannot see.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_mcp_soft_digest.py::test_facade_mode_still_compares_prompts_because_clients_see_them_either_way

chunk_findings.detail:
`items` is only compared when the new `items` is a non-empty dict. A JSON Schema tightening to `items: false` is therefore skipped as a no-op. Example: old tool `inputSchema` is
`{"type":"object","properties":{"xs":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}}}}`
and new is identical except `xs.items` is `false`. The call `{"xs":["a"]}` is valid under old and invalid under new, so `schema_problems` must be non-empty. It returns `[]`, so `_diff_tools` records the tool change as `"description or schema extended"` in `additive`, and `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES)` returns soft rung 3 for a breaking tightening.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:schema_problems

chunk_findings.detail:
`additionalProperties` changing from `false` (or omitted, which this code itself treats as `True`) to `{}` is reported as `"additionalProperties restricted"`, but `{}` accepts every additional-property value, so the change is loosening or even equivalent. Old
`{"type":"object","properties":{"a":{"type":"string"}},"additionalProperties":false}`
and new identical except `additionalProperties` is `{}`: every valid old call is still valid. The final `return [f"{where}: additionalProperties restricted"]` runs because `now` is a dict while `was` is a bool. The earlier false -> `true` fix does not cover false/omitted -> `{}`, and `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES)` still returns hard rung 5 for a compatible change.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_additional_problems

chunk_findings.detail: A surface that appears is omitted from the returned `pending` list, even for a client that ignores `list_changed`. For `old={"flat": s}` and `new={"flat": s, "profile": p}` with `client=IGNORES`, the new-surface branch returns `Verdict("soft", 3, ("added",), honours)` using the default `pending=()`, so the final `pending` is empty. But `Verdict.pending` is documented as what an ignoring client sees only after a restart; a newly-added surface is exactly such an item, and single-surface `classify` already places additive tools in `pending`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:classify_surfaces

chunk_findings.detail:
The `_EXACT`, `_LOWER_BOUNDS`, and `_UPPER_BOUNDS` loops compare keywords without considering the schema instance type, so they report restrictions that cannot reject a single old-valid value. For tool `inputSchema`
old `{"type":"object","properties":{"n":{"type":"integer","pattern":"a"}}}`
and new identical except `pattern` is `"b"`: `pattern` applies only to strings, so every integer `n` valid under old is still valid. `_constraint_problems` nonetheless appends `"n: pattern changed"`, and `classify(old, new, client=IGNORES)` returns hard rung 5 for a non-breaking change. The earlier test-side probe for tightened/loosened bounds does not exercise this production path.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/surfaces/ifacedigest.py:_constraint_problems

chunk_findings.detail: `output_problems` does not perform the same conservative constraint checks as `schema_problems`. chunk_findings.detail: The `gate` that releases the in-flight `slow` handler is only set after `yield WP.encode(WP.drain())` executes and the worker then asks the `Feed` iterator for the next item. But a worker implementing the required drain behavior reads `drain` and blocks waiting for that in-flight handler before asking for more input. As a result, `gate.set()` is not reached while the worker is blocked; `slow` only continues because its own `gate.wait(5)` times out five seconds later. chunk_findings.detail: The assertion `order[0] == 2` depends on thread scheduling, not just on requests being served independently. chunk_findings.detail: After a `drain` frame, the drain thread is required to send `drained` and then `bye`. If that call is scheduled before the drain thread's `self.write(WP.drained())`, the wire sees `bye` before `drained`, violating the contract. For example, frames `[hello, drain]` followed by EOF can emit `bye("eof")` before `drained`; a shim that treats `bye` as final can lose the `drained` frame.

chunk_findings.detail: `run_worker` creates `threading.Thread(target=worker.run, ...)` without `daemon=True`. If `worker.run` ever fails to exit at EOF—the exact condition the helper’s `assert not t.is_alive()` is meant to report—the assertion raises, but the non-daemon worker thread keeps running. At interpreter shutdown Python waits for non-daemon threads, so the pytest process can hang after the failure is already reported, and the run never delivers a clean exit code. The failed ingress leaves a live non-daemon thread; make it a daemon thread or run the worker in a terminable way.

chunk_findings.detail: When `run()` exits without appending a value to `code` (an unhandled exception escaped before the post-loop append) and `done` is set by a drain finishing, this line returns 0, misclassifying a crash as a clean exit. The main loop can be inside `t.join(0.1)` when `finish` writes `bye` and sets `done`; if the run thread then dies without appending to `code`, the loop exits with `t.is_alive()` false, `code == []`, and `done.is_set()` true, so `return 0 if done.is_set() else 1` returns 0. The comment itself says an empty `code` may mean `run()` died, but the expression only returns 1 when `done` is false. A dead run thread with no status is still a crash, so the branch should only return 0 for a clean drain when `t.is_alive()` is true (or otherwise distinguish clean drain from crash).

chunk_findings.detail: The replacement guard still returns 0 for a crash in one interleaving. `Thread.is_alive()` is true not only when `run` is healthily blocked after a completed drain; CPython also leaves `is_alive()` true while it is unwinding an unhandled exception and running `sys.excepthook`, before the thread object is marked stopped. chunk_findings.detail: The new “say so rather than go silent” path catches only `TypeError` and `ValueError` from `WP.encode`. Python’s JSON encoder raises `RecursionError` when a payload is nested deeper than the recursion limit, and `RecursionError` is not a subclass of `ValueError`. Given a request whose handler returns such a deeply nested value, `WP.encode(response)` raises `RecursionError`, no error frame is written, and the exception escapes `write`; the worker crashes instead of sending the intended error frame and leaves the live request unanswered.

chunk_findings.detail: `finish()` writes `WP.drained()` and then `self.bye("drained")` as two separate `write` calls with no intervening guard. The main `run` loop is still reading and can concurrently call `r.write` for a malformed/surprising frame after `drain`. If the drain thread wins the first write, the main loop can emit `bad_frame` after `drained` but before `bye`, producing `drained`, then `error`, then `bye` — an error frame interleaved between `drained` and `bye`. The missive says drain finishes in-flight work then `drained+bye`; the new `said_bye` guard only suppresses frames after `bye` is set, so it does not close this pre-`bye` gap.

chunk_findings.detail: `decode` catches only `ValueError` around `json.loads`, but `json.loads` can raise `RecursionError` for deeply nested JSON (for example `'[' * 2000 + '1' + ']' * 2000`, which exceeds the default recursion limit). chunk_findings.detail: `_internal_error` answers both “no `id` member” and `"id": null` with `None` because `msg.get("id") is None` is true for both. A JSON-RPC notification is only a request *without* an `id`; a request with `"id": null` is still a request and is owed a JSON-RPC response with `"id": null`. For a `req` carrying `{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":null,"method":"..."}` whose handler raises, `_internal_error` returns `None`, and `serve` writes `WP.response(rid, None)`. Per the protocol, a `res` with a null msg acknowledges a notification, so the shim does not receive the required JSON-RPC internal-error response for this live request.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `main` still lets a crash be misreported as exit 0. If a drain has set `done`, `main` waits only `t.join(0.2)`; when the `run` thread is still alive after that timeout because its own crash-reporting `print(traceback.format_exc(), file=sys.stderr)` is blocked (for example stderr is a pipe the shim is not reading), `code` is still empty and `done.is_set()` is true, so this line returns 0. The target’s own `except BaseException` would otherwise append 1, but process exits 0, masking a crashed `run` as a completed drain. A finite 0.2s join cannot distinguish that crash from the intended “stdin still open after a clean drain” case.

chunk_findings.detail: `worker_protocol.hello` accepts any `state_key: str`, and the protocol docstring only says `{shim_proto, state_key?}` with no hex restriction, but `negotiate` returns `error("bad_frame", "`state_key` must be a hex string")` for any non-even-length/non-hex value. chunk_findings.detail: `decode` can accept a malformed `hello` instead of raising `ProtocolError`, despite its contract that anything that is not a valid frame is an error. The worker-hello required `digest`/`version` string check runs only when `worker_proto` is present and `shim_proto` is absent; adding any `shim_proto` key makes the check skip. The final `any(_int(...))` check then passes if `worker_proto` is an int. Concretely, `decode('{"t":"hello","shim_proto":"bad","worker_proto":1}')` returns that dict, but this is not a valid hello in either direction: a worker hello must carry string `digest` and `version`, and they are missing. The shared decoder is the validator the shim is supposed to use, so a malformed worker hello can get past frame validation.

chunk_findings.detail: `capability` only honours an explicit runtime observation when `observed in (HONOURS, IGNORES)`. But `UNKNOWN` is a valid observed value, and the module contract says a runtime observation overrides the table and returns “what it saw”. Given `client_info={"name": "opencode"}`, `observed=UNKNOWN`, and `today=date(2026,10,21)`, the function falls through to the table and returns `"honours"`; an observed-unknown client that should be treated as hard is wrongly treated as soft.

chunk_findings.detail: `_BY_NAME` is built only from `e.names`, so every row using the default `names=()` cannot be reached by `lookup`/`capability`. For example the `kimi` row has `key="kimi"` and `list_changed=IGNORES`, but `lookup({"name": "kimi"})` returns `None`, so `capability({"name": "kimi"})` returns `UNKNOWN` instead of `IGNORES`. The same applies to documented honours/ignores rows such as `vscode-copilot`, `openhands`, `grok-cli`, `cursor-cli`, `windsurf`, etc. The module contract says the table is keyed by the lower-cased `clientInfo.name`; those rows must be indexed by their client name (or `_BY_NAME` must include `entry.key` when `names` is empty).

chunk_findings.detail: The runtime observation override only checks `observed in (HONOURS, IGNORES)`, so `observed="unknown"` does not override the table even though `UNKNOWN` is a valid `LIST_CHANGED` result and the module doc says a runtime observation returns “what it saw”. Concrete failure: `capability({"name": "claude-code", "version": "2.1.296"}, observed="unknown")` returns `HONOURS` from the table rather than `UNKNOWN`, so a failed/unknown observation cannot prevent a stale honours answer. It should return any valid observed value, e.g. `if observed in LIST_CHANGED: return observed`.

chunk_findings.detail: The module docstring states that `MAX_AGE_DAYS` is “a window on the data, not a user tunable”, but `capability` exposes `max_age_days` as a keyword argument. A caller can pass a huge value, e.g. `capability({"name": "opencode"}, today=date(2027, 6, 1), max_age_days=999999)`. The unverified `opencode` honours row was checked 2026-10-21 and must return `"unknown"` after the 180-day window (2027-04-19); with `max_age_days=999999` it returns `"honours"`, bypassing the documented fixed safety window and reporting the wrong capability for a documented client.
